lessons.unit: Animals including humans
lessons.title: Nutrition and food groups
objectives: Explain why animals including humans need nutrition
Name the main food groups and give examples
Explain that animals cannot make their own food

keywords.def: the food and nutrients animals need to live and grow
foods that give energy, such as bread and rice
food for growth and repair, such as fish and beans
foods that store energy and keep us warm, like oil

starter: Bismillah. Say the stages in a plant's life cycle.
Why can't animals make their own food like plants do?
What did you have for breakfast?

teach.heading: Why we need food
teach.note: Ask 'What happens if a car has no fuel?' compare to a body with no food. Animals cannot make their own food, so they eat plants or other animals.

teach.heading: Food groups
teach.note: Show photos. Link to Qur'an 7:31 (eat and drink, but do not be wasteful). Keep ethos light: we thank Allah for food by saying Bismillah before eating and Alhamdulillah after.

teach.heading: Vitamins, minerals, fibre and water
bullets: Vitamins and minerals keep us healthy
teach.note: Fruit and vegetables give vitamins; milk gives calcium for bones. Misconception: fat is always bad; we need some fat.

teach.heading: Sorting foods
bullets: Some foods fit more than one group
teach.note: Safe task: children look through the kitchen cupboards (with a grown-up) and read labels, or use pictures. Do not taste unknown items. Check allergies.

practice: Which food group does rice belong to?
Name a food that gives us protein.
Why do we need water every day?
independent: Sort 12 foods (such as bread, egg, apple, olive oil, lentils, fish, rice, yoghurt, nuts, carrot, pasta, beans) into food groups.
Write two sentences: why do animals need food?
Design a healthy lunch for a child and label the food groups in it.
exit: Name the food group that gives energy.
Why can't animals make their own food?
lessons.homework: Record everything you eat at lunch and dinner and sort it into food groups.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use picture sorting cards with key words. Stretch: explain why athletes may need more carbohydrates.

lessons.title: Friction: why do things slow down?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a toy car stop on a carpet but roll far on a smooth floor?
objectives: To understand that friction is a force that slows moving things down
successCriteria: All: say that friction is a force between two surfaces
Most: predict which surface gives more friction
Some: explain why rough surfaces slow things more than smooth ones
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: comparing distances in centimetres
lessons.smsc: Social: taking turns and sharing equipment safely at home

keywords.def: a push or a pull
a force that slows things when two surfaces rub
the top or outside layer of something
bumpy, not smooth
flat and even, with no bumps

hook.text: Why is it easy to slide in socks on a shiny floor but hard on a carpet?
hook.a: The carpet is rough, so there is more friction. The shiny floor is smooth, so there is less.

islamicLink.text: Allah made the earth firm under our feet so we can walk on it. Allah says He made the earth a resting place for us (al-Baqarah 2:22). Friction is part of this mercy: without it we could not walk, hold a cup or stop a bike.

starter.q: Is a kick a push or a pull?
Name one force that pulls things down to the ground.
Opening a drawer: push or pull?

teach.heading: What is friction?
bullets: It happens when two surfaces rub
teach.note: Rub your hands together fast. Ask: what do you feel? Warmth and a grip. That grip is friction.

teach.heading: Rough and smooth
bullets: More friction means a shorter journey
teach.note: Show a towel and a tray on camera. Ask pupils to touch two surfaces at home and say which is rougher.

teach.heading: Friction helps us
teach.note: Ask: where is friction useful in your home? Where is it a nuisance, like a sticking door?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds, then share results.

check.q: A toy car rolls on four surfaces. Where will it go furthest?
check.why: The smooth floor has the least friction, so the car travels furthest.

practice.q: A ball rolls on grass and on a smooth path. Where does it stop sooner?
practice.a: On the grass: it is rougher, so there is more friction.
practice.model:
Think: which surface is rougher?
Grass is rougher.
Rough means more friction.
More friction slows the ball sooner.
So it stops sooner on the grass.

practice.q: Is friction a push or a pull, or something else?
practice.a: It is a force that works against movement (it pushes back against the way something moves).

practice.q: Name one place where friction is useful.
practice.a: For example: shoe soles, bike brakes, tyres, holding a pencil.

independent.q: Core: Push a toy car or a small box across three surfaces at home (a towel, the floor, a tray). Write them in order, most friction first.
independent.a: For example: towel, floor, tray (rough to smooth).
independent.model:
Teacher shows it first: same toy, same gentle push, three surfaces.
Most friction is where it stops soonest.

independent.q: Extend: Why did the toy stop soonest on the roughest surface?
independent.a: Rough surfaces rub more, so there is more friction slowing it.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do people put salt or grit on icy paths?
independent.a: To make the path rougher, so shoes get more friction and people do not slip.

exit.q: Which gives more friction?
exit.a: A) a towel

exit.q: Big question: why does a toy car stop on a carpet but roll far on a smooth floor?
exit.a: The carpet is rough, so there is more friction slowing the car.

lessons.homework: Find three things at home that use friction to help us (for example shoe soles) and draw or write them in your book.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards of surfaces to sort into rough and smooth. EAL: rough, smooth, slow with pictures. Stretch: think of a place where we want less friction and how we make it smoother.

lessons.title: Friction fair test: the ramp investigation
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we make our friction test fair?
objectives: To understand how to run a fair test to compare friction on different surfaces
successCriteria: All: measure how far a toy rolls off a ramp
Most: keep the ramp, toy and push the same each time
Some: use the results table to write a conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: measuring in centimetres and reading a table
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty: recording what really happened, not what we hoped

keywords.def: a test where we change only one thing
find out how big or long something is
a slope for things to roll down
what we found out
a force that slows things when surfaces rub

hook.text: If you rolled a toy car down a ramp onto a towel and pushed it harder than on the floor, would it be a fair race?
hook.a: No. Only one thing should change: the surface. The push must stay the same.

starter.q: What is friction?
starter.a: A force that slows things when two surfaces rub.

starter.q: Which has more friction?
Write 1 m in centimetres.

teach.heading: Our question
bullets: Which surface lets the car roll furthest?
teach.note: Build the ramp live: a tray resting on two books. Point out what we will keep the same.

teach.heading: Keep it fair
teach.note: Ask: what would happen if we pushed the car on one surface? It would not be fair.

teach.heading: Safety first
bullets: Ask an adult before moving books
Keep the toy away from stairs
teach.note: Read the safety card together. Tidy away when finished.

teach.heading: Record in a table
teach.note: Model the table on screen.

practice.q: From the table, which surface let the car roll furthest?
practice.a: The floor (120 cm and 116 cm).
practice.model:
Look down the columns for the biggest numbers.
Floor: 120 and 116.
These are the biggest, so the car went furthest on the floor.

practice.q: Which surface had the most friction?
practice.a: The towel: the car only rolled about 30 cm.

practice.q: Name one thing we kept the same.
practice.a: For example: the same car, the same ramp height, letting go without pushing.

independent.q: Core: Do the ramp test at home on 3 surfaces (floor, paper, a towel or cardboard). Record two goes each in your table.
independent.a: Pupils' own results; the towel usually gives the shortest distance.
independent.model: Teacher shows one go on camera: put the car at the top line, let go, measure from the ramp end to the front of the car with a ruler or tape, write it down.

independent.q: Extend: Write a conclusion: 'The car rolled furthest on ... because ...'
independent.a: For example: The car rolled furthest on the floor because it is smooth and has the least friction.

independent.q: Stretch: Why did we do each surface twice?
independent.a: To check our results; if the two goes are close, we can trust them more.

exit.q: In a fair test, how many things do we change?
exit.a: A) one

exit.q: Big question: how can we make our friction test fair?
exit.a: Change only the surface; keep the car, ramp height and release the same.

lessons.homework: Finish your ramp table and write one sentence about which surface had the most friction.
lessons.send: SEND: a ready-made table and a partner adult to measure. EAL: same, change, measure with gestures. Stretch: predict what happens if the ramp is made higher, and why.

lessons.title: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes something stick to a magnet?
objectives: To understand that only some materials are magnetic
successCriteria: All: sort objects into magnetic and non-magnetic
Most: say that magnetic objects contain iron or steel
Some: explain why not all metals are magnetic
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: magnetic catches on doors and lunch boxes
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the hidden forces Allah placed in creation

keywords.def: an object that pulls iron and steel towards it
pulled by a magnet
not pulled by a magnet
what something is made of
a hard, shiny material such as iron or copper

hook.text: Is every metal pulled by a magnet? How could you find out at home?
hook.a: No. Test spoons, foil, coins and cans with a fridge magnet and see.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for people' (al-Hadid 57:25). Iron is the main metal that magnets pull, and we use it in tools, buildings and magnets.

starter.q: What does friction do to a moving toy?
In a fair test, how many things do we change?
Name a metal.
starter.a: For example: iron, steel, copper, aluminium, gold.

teach.heading: What do magnets do?
teach.note: Hold a fridge magnet to a paper clip on camera. Then to a pencil. Ask what is different.

teach.heading: Make a prediction
teach.note: Show a spoon, a coin, foil, a key. Pupils predict before you test.

teach.heading: Sort the objects
teach.note: Read each card. Pupils show 1 or 2 on fingers.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds, then share results.

check.q: Which is magnetic?
check.why: Steel contains iron, so the paper clip is pulled by the magnet.

practice.q: Is a wooden spoon magnetic?
practice.a: No, wood is non-magnetic.
practice.model:
Ask: is it made of iron or steel?
Wood is not.
So the magnet will not pull it.
It is non-magnetic.

practice.q: Is a steel spoon magnetic?
practice.a: Yes, most steel is magnetic because it contains iron.

practice.q: Finish: 'Magnetic objects are usually made of ...'
practice.a: iron or steel

independent.q: Core: Test 8 objects at home with a fridge magnet. Sort them in a two-column table: magnetic and non-magnetic.
independent.a: Pupils' own; steel and iron objects are magnetic, plastic, wood, glass and fabric are not.
independent.model:
Teacher shows it first: hold the magnet close to a key, a sock and a tin.
Write each in the right column.

independent.q: Extend: Did any results surprise you? Write one.
independent.a: For example: foil is a metal but was not magnetic.

independent.q: Stretch: Write a rule that fits all your results.
independent.a: For example: things made of iron or steel are magnetic; other materials are not.

exit.q: Are all metals magnetic?
exit.a: B) no

exit.q: Big question: what makes something stick to a magnet?
exit.a: It is made of a magnetic material such as iron or steel.

lessons.homework: Find five magnetic things on your fridge or around your kitchen (with an adult) and list them.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects and a two-hoop sort. EAL: magnet, magnetic, non-magnetic with pictures. Stretch: test a coin and say what it might be made of.

lessons.title: Which metals are magnetic? The kitchen sort
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a magnet pick up a steel spoon but not an aluminium can?
objectives: To understand that iron and steel are magnetic but metals such as aluminium and copper are not
successCriteria: All: name iron and steel as magnetic metals
Most: sort kitchen metals into magnetic and non-magnetic
Some: use a magnet to sort cans for recycling and explain how it works
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: how recycling centres sort metals
lessons.smsc: Moral: looking after Allah's earth by recycling and not wasting

keywords.def: a strong metal that magnets pull
a metal made mostly from iron
a light metal that magnets do not pull
an orange-brown metal that magnets do not pull
use materials again to make new things

hook.text: A recycling centre has a huge pile of mixed cans. How could a magnet help to sort them?
hook.a: Steel cans stick to a big magnet; aluminium cans do not, so they can be separated.

islamicLink.text: Allah taught the Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) to work with iron and make coats of armour (Saba 34:10-11). Learning which metals are strong and magnetic helps us use Allah's gifts wisely.

starter.q: Is plastic magnetic?
Name a magnetic metal.
What is the opposite of magnetic?

teach.heading: Not all metals
teach.note: Show a foil sheet: shiny metal, but the magnet does not pull it.

teach.heading: Kitchen metals
teach.note: Ask pupils which they might find in their own kitchen.

teach.heading: Sorting cans
teach.note: Explain recycling centres use giant magnets on conveyor belts.
cycle: A big magnet lifts steel cans
Aluminium cans stay on the belt
Each metal is melted and reused

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds, then share results.

check.q: Which can will a magnet pick up?
check.why: Steel contains iron, so it is magnetic. Aluminium and copper are metals but not magnetic.

practice.q: Is aluminium foil magnetic?
practice.a: No. Aluminium is a metal but it is not magnetic.
practice.model: Step 1: what metal is it? Aluminium. Step 2: is aluminium magnetic? No. So foil is not pulled by a magnet.

practice.q: Is a steel food tin magnetic?
practice.a: Yes, steel contains iron.

practice.q: True or false: all shiny metals are magnetic.
practice.a: False: aluminium and copper are shiny but not magnetic.

independent.q: Core: With an adult, test 6 metal things in the kitchen (tin, foil, spoon, pan, key, coin). Record magnetic or not.
independent.a: Pupils' own; steel tins and most steel spoons are magnetic, foil is not.
independent.model:
Teacher shows it first: test a tin (sticks: steel) and foil (does not stick: aluminium).
Write both in the table.

independent.q: Extend: Explain how a magnet could sort steel and aluminium cans.
independent.a: The magnet pulls the steel cans out; the aluminium cans are left behind.

independent.q: Stretch: A pan is not pulled by the magnet. What metal might it be? Why?
independent.a: Aluminium or copper, because those metals are not magnetic.

exit.q: Which metal is NOT magnetic?
exit.a: C) aluminium

exit.q: Big question: why does a magnet pick up a steel spoon but not an aluminium can?
exit.a: Steel contains iron, which is magnetic; aluminium is not.

lessons.homework: With an adult, check your recycling bin: which items would a magnet pick up? Write a list.
lessons.send: SEND: real cans and foil to test, with picture labels. EAL: iron, steel, aluminium, copper on a word mat. Stretch: find out why steel tins are used for food.

lessons.title: Magnets attract and repel: poles
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a magnet push something without touching it?
objectives: To understand that magnets have two poles and can attract or repel without touching
successCriteria: All: name the north and south poles of a magnet
Most: say that like poles repel and unlike poles attract
Some: show that magnetic forces act at a distance and through paper
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the north and south of a compass
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at an invisible force we cannot see but can feel

keywords.def: the end of a magnet where the force is strongest
pull towards
push away
one end of a magnet, often marked N
the other end of a magnet, often marked S

hook.text: You can feel two magnets push apart, but there is nothing between them. What is pushing?
hook.a: The magnetic force acts at a distance. It does not need touching.

starter.q: Is a steel paper clip magnetic?
Name a metal that is not magnetic.
What is a force?

teach.heading: Two poles
bullets: Every magnet has a north and a south pole
The force is strongest at the poles
teach.note: Show a bar magnet with N and S. Paper clips cling most at the ends.

teach.heading: Attract or repel?
bullets: Like poles repel: N and N, S and S
Unlike poles attract: N and S
teach.note: If pupils have two fridge magnets, try them back to back.

teach.heading: Force at a distance
bullets: Magnets do not need to touch
teach.note: Hold a paper clip under paper, move a magnet above it. The clip moves. Contact forces, like friction, need touching.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds, then share results.

check.q: Two north poles are brought together. What happens?
check.why: Like poles repel.

practice.q: N and S are put together. Attract or repel?
practice.a: Attract (unlike poles).
practice.model:
Are the poles the same or different?
N and S are different.
Different poles attract.
So they pull together.

practice.q: S and S are put together. Attract or repel?
practice.a: Repel (like poles).

practice.q: Does a magnet need to touch a paper clip to move it?
practice.a: No: magnetic force acts at a distance.

independent.q: Core: Put a paper clip on paper. Move a magnet underneath without touching the clip. Write what happens.
independent.a: The paper clip moves with the magnet: the force works through the paper.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first on camera, then pupils try it.

independent.q: Extend: Try through 1, 2, then 5 sheets of paper. Does it still work?
independent.a: It works through a few sheets but gets weaker as the gap grows.

independent.q: Stretch: Why might a magnet not hold a heavy drawing on the fridge?
independent.a: The force is not strong enough to hold the weight, especially with a gap.

exit.q: Like poles...
exit.a: B) repel

exit.q: Big question: how can a magnet push something without touching it?
exit.a: Magnetic force acts at a distance; like poles repel.

lessons.homework: Draw a bar magnet and label N and S. Draw arrows to show two magnets attracting and two repelling.
lessons.send: SEND: coloured N and S cards to match. EAL: attract and repel with hand actions. Stretch: test how far away a magnet can still move a paper clip, in centimetres.

lessons.title: How strong is a magnet? Uses of magnets
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a bigger magnet always a stronger magnet?
objectives: To understand how to compare the strength of magnets and how we use magnets every day
successCriteria: All: count how many paper clips a magnet holds
Most: compare two magnets fairly
Some: explain why the biggest magnet is not always the strongest
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: tally and bar chart of paper clip counts
lessons.smsc: Social: working with an adult and sharing results with the class

keywords.def: how strongly a magnet pulls
look at how things are the same or different
things linked one after another
what we think will happen
pulled by a magnet

hook.text: You have a big magnet and a tiny magnet. Which is stronger? How could you test it fairly?
hook.a: Size does not always tell us. Count how many paper clips each can hold in a chain.

starter.q: Like poles: attract or repel?
Can a magnet work through paper?
Name a magnetic metal.

teach.heading: Test the strength
bullets: Hang a paper clip from the magnet
Add clips one at a time
Count the clips before they fall
teach.note: Model the chain test on camera.

teach.heading: Keep it fair
teach.note: Ask: what must stay the same?

teach.heading: Example results
bullets: More clips means a stronger magnet
teach.note: Point out the small round magnet beat the big flat one.

teach.heading: Magnets we use
teach.note: Ask pupils to find one magnet in their home.

practice.q: Magnet A held 4 clips. Magnet B held 10 clips. Which is stronger?
practice.a: Magnet B: it held more clips.
practice.model:
Compare the numbers: 10 is more than 4.
More clips held means a stronger pull.
So magnet B is stronger.

practice.q: In the bar chart, which magnet was weakest?
practice.a: The fridge magnet (2 clips).

practice.q: Why must the paper clips be the same size?
practice.a: So the test is fair; bigger clips are heavier.

independent.q: Core: Test two magnets at home with the paper clip chain. Record the number of clips for each.
independent.a: Pupils' own results.
independent.model:
Teacher shows it first: one clip, then two, then three, until the chain drops.
The last number that stayed is the result.

independent.q: Extend: Which magnet was stronger? Was it the bigger one?
independent.a: Pupils' own; the bigger magnet is not always the stronger one.

independent.q: Stretch: Name two uses of magnets in your home and say why a magnet is useful there.
independent.a: For example: fridge door seal keeps the door shut; bag clasp holds the bag closed without a zip.

exit.q: More paper clips held means the magnet is...
exit.a: A) stronger

exit.q: Big question: is a bigger magnet always a stronger magnet?
exit.a: No. We must test it; some small magnets are very strong.

lessons.homework: Find three uses of magnets at home and draw one of them with a label.
lessons.send: SEND: count clips with an adult; number line to 20. EAL: stronger, weaker, compare. Stretch: draw a bar chart of your results.

lessons.title: Light sources: why do cat's eyes glow?
lessons.bigQuestion: Do cat's eyes really make their own light?
objectives: To understand that we need light to see and that some things give out light while others only reflect it
successCriteria: All: name three light sources
Most: say that dark is the absence of light
Some: explain why cat's eyes and the Moon are not light sources
lessons.crossCurricular: English: Cornerstones companion text question 'Why do cat's eyes glow at night?'
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah made the Sun a lamp and the Moon a reflected light

keywords.def: something that gives out its own light
where there is no light
bounce light off a surface
light enters our eyes
give out light

hook.text: In a room with no light at all, could a cat see a mouse? Could you?
hook.a: No. Cats need some light too. With no light at all, nothing can be seen.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'It is He who made the sun a shining light and the moon a derived light' (Yunus 10:5). The Sun makes its own light; the Moon only shines because it reflects the Sun's light.

starter.q: Name a use of magnets.
starter.a: For example: fridge door, compass, sorting cans.

starter.q: Is the Sun a light source?
What do we need to see?

teach.heading: Light sources
bullets: A light source gives out its own light
The Sun, a torch, a lamp, a candle
teach.note: Ask: which things in your room give out light?

teach.heading: How we see
teach.note: Draw arrows: Sun to book, book to eye. Ask: where does the light start?

teach.heading: Cat's eyes
bullets: A shiny layer reflects light back
teach.note: Cats see well in dim light; a layer at the back of the eye reflects light. Road studs work the same way.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds.

check.q: Which is a light source?
check.why: A torch gives out its own light. The others reflect light.

practice.q: Is the Moon a light source?
practice.a: No. It reflects light from the Sun.
practice.model:
Ask: does it make its own light?
The Moon does not.
It shines because the Sun's light bounces off it.
So it is not a light source.

practice.q: What is dark?
practice.a: When there is no light.

practice.q: Put in order: light enters eye, light leaves Sun, light hits book.
practice.a: Light leaves Sun, light hits book, light enters eye.

independent.q: Core: Go around your home (with an adult). List 4 light sources and 4 things that only reflect light.
independent.a: Light sources: lamp, screen, torch, oven light. Reflect only: mirror, spoon, foil, window.

hook.text: A sycamore seed has 'wings' and a burdock seed has tiny hooks. Why do you think seeds have such different shapes?
hook.a: Each shape helps the seed travel a different way: wings for wind, hooks to catch on animal fur.

islamicLink.text: Allah tells us that He inspired the bee to make its homes in mountains, trees and what people build, and to eat from all the fruits (An-Nahl 16:68-69). As bees feed, they carry pollen from flower to flower.

practice.q: Explain how a bee helps a flower make seeds.
practice.a: Pollen sticks to the bee and rubs onto another flower's stigma, so seeds can form
practice.model: Two steps: 'Pollen sticks to the bee when it drinks nectar. The bee carries it to another flower's stigma, so that flower can make seeds.'

practice.q: How does a blackberry seed travel?
practice.a: An animal eats the fruit and drops the seed somewhere else

practice.q: Why do seeds need to travel?
practice.a: To find light, water and space away from the parent plant

independent.q: Core: With an adult, cut open a fruit (apple, tomato or pea pod). Draw the seeds inside and write how they might travel.
independent.a: A labelled drawing of seeds in the fruit and a dispersal method, e.g. animals eat apples
independent.model: Teacher shows a pea pod opened on camera, counts the peas and says 'the pod pops open to spread them'.

independent.q: Extend: Make a paper sycamore spinner. Drop it from the same height with and without wings. What do you notice?
independent.a: With wings it falls slower and spins, so wind can carry it further

independent.q: Stretch: Design a seed that travels by water. Label its features.
independent.a: For example: light, waterproof, hollow so it floats

exit.q: Pollen moving from stamen to stigma is...
exit.a: Pollination

exit.q: Big question: why do seeds have different shapes?
exit.a: Each shape helps the seed travel a different way: wings or parachutes for wind, hooks for fur.
